usamts-2017-r1-01.prompt:
Fill each white square in with a number so that each of the 27 three-digit numbers whose digits are all 1, 2, or 3 is used exactly once. Some numbers have been given to you (see the figure; below it the 27 numbers are listed with the given ones crossed out).

In the table below, $\blacksquare$ marks a black square and an empty corner position (top-left three and bottom-right three) is not part of the grid:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline  &  &  & \phantom{000} & \phantom{000} & 212 & \phantom{000} & \phantom{000}\\\hline \phantom{000} & \blacksquare & \phantom{000} & 213 & \blacksquare & \phantom{000} & \blacksquare & 123\\\hline \phantom{000} & \blacksquare & \phantom{000} & \phantom{000} & \phantom{000} & \phantom{000} & 131 & \phantom{000}\\\hline \phantom{000} & \blacksquare & 121 & \blacksquare & \phantom{000} & 113 & \blacksquare & \phantom{000}\\\hline \phantom{000} & \phantom{000} & \phantom{000} & \phantom{000} & 312 &  &  & \\\hline\end{array}$$

usamts-2017-r1-02.prompt: After each Goober ride, the driver rates the passenger as 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 stars. The passenger's overall rating is determined as the average of all of the ratings given to him or her by drivers so far. Noah had been on several rides, and his rating was neither 1 nor 5. Then he got a 1 star on a ride because he barfed on the driver. Show that the number of 5 stars that Noah needs in order to climb back to at least his overall rating before barfing is independent of the number of rides that he had taken.
usamts-2017-r1-02.answer: If his rating was $r$ after $k$ rides, he needs the least $n$ with $\frac{kr + 1 + 5n}{k + 1 + n} \ge r \iff 1 + 5n \ge r(n+1)$, i.e. $n = \left\lceil \frac{r-1}{5-r} \right\rceil$, which does not involve $k$.

usamts-2017-r1-03.prompt: Do there exist two polygons such that, by putting them together in three different ways (without holes, overlap, or reflections), we can obtain first a triangle, then a convex quadrilateral, and lastly a convex pentagon?
usamts-2017-r1-03.answer: **Yes.** Cut a 30-60-90 triangle with legs $\sqrt3, 1$ by the perpendicular to the hypotenuse at its midpoint: a 30-60-90 triangle (legs $1$, $\frac1{\sqrt3}$) and a kite with sides $\frac1{\sqrt3}, 1, 1, \frac1{\sqrt3}$ and angles $120^\circ, 90^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$. Rotating the small triangle gives a convex quadrilateral and a convex pentagon.

usamts-2017-r1-04.prompt: Two players take turns placing an unused number from $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$ into one of the empty squares in a $2 \times 4$ array (a top row of 4 squares and a bottom row of 4 squares). The game ends once all the squares are filled. The first player wins if the product of the numbers in the top row is greater. The second player wins if the product of the numbers in the bottom row is greater. If both players play with perfect strategy, who wins this game?
usamts-2017-r1-04.answer: **The first player wins**: he puts 1 in the bottom row; the second player must then put 2 in the top row (else the first player puts 2 in the bottom); then the first player puts 3 in the bottom row, and the bottom product is at most $1\cdot3\cdot7\cdot8 = 168 < 240 = 2\cdot4\cdot5\cdot6 \le$ top product.

usamts-2017-r1-05.prompt: Does there exist a set $S$ consisting of rational numbers with the following property? For every integer $n$ there is a unique nonempty, finite subset of $S$, whose elements sum to $n$.
usamts-2017-r1-05.answer: **Yes.** List the integers as $s_1, s_2, s_3, \dots$ and take $S = \{-10^{-k} : k \ge 1\} \cup \{s_k + 0.\underbrace{1\ldots1}_{k} : k \ge 1\}$; then $n = s_k$ is uniquely $\left(s_k + 0.1\ldots1\right) - 0.1 - 0.01 - \dots - 10^{-k}$.
